name: Ascendant Psychology
description: Defines orientation-related needs, sensitivities, defensive strategies, regulation needs, blind spots, and integration markers.

coreNeed.definition: A sufficiently coherent and flexible way to position the self at the beginning of contact with people, situations, and environments.

coreMotivation.definition: Create an initial orientation that allows engagement to begin without requiring the first response to define the entire interaction.

coreSensitivity.definition: Heightened awareness of how situations begin and how quickly orientation must be established.
Heightened awareness of how posture, pacing, tone, and presence are read at first contact.
Heightened awareness of whether the immediate environment supports or disrupts the preferred orientation.
Heightened awareness of where the self stands relative to others, expectations, and thresholds.

coreFearPatterns.definition: Fear of entering a situation from an unworkable or misunderstood position.
Fear that the initial presentation will become a fixed judgment of identity.
Fear that the environment or another person will define the terms of engagement before self-positioning is established.
Fear of being required to engage before enough situational information is available.

protectiveStrategies.definition: Manage posture, tone, pacing, or visibility in order to reduce uncertainty at entry.
Adopt a fixed approach before enough contextual information is available.
Conceal or alter presentation when the preferred orientation feels unsafe or unacceptable.
Delay or avoid engagement when a workable self-position cannot be established.
Treat the initial orientation as proof of the entire self.

blindSpots: Confusing first response with permanent identity
Overestimating the importance of first impressions
Underestimating how much orientation changes after contact begins
Mistaking environmental mismatch for personal inadequacy
Using one orientation in every context
Assuming others perceive the intended presentation accurately

regulationNeeds.definition: Allow the initial frame to update as new information becomes available.
Keep observable presentation distinct from total identity.
Gather enough environmental information before fixing the orientation.
Match the speed of engagement to the available capacity and context.
Include the relational counterpart rather than organizing entry from the self-side alone.

healthyPsychologicalFunctions: Position the self without erasing the counterpart
Enter situations with enough agency and flexibility
Use embodiment as information rather than proof of identity
Distinguish immediate salience from final judgment
Coordinate Ascendant and Descendant reference frames
integrationMarkers: Can revise first impressions without identity threat
Can enter unfamiliar situations without rigid presentation control
Can let posture and presentation vary by context
Can notice the counterpart while maintaining self-position
Can allow engagement to reshape the starting frame
reflectionComponents: What orientation am I establishing here?
What information do I not yet have?
Is this presentation functional, defensive, or habitual?
What would allow me to enter with more flexibility?
Am I treating first contact as the whole relationship?
How is the counterpart changing the frame?
psychologyConstraints: No personality diagnosis may be inferred from the Ascendant.
No appearance claim may be treated as guaranteed.
The Descendant must remain available as the opposite reference frame.
Developmental language must reference the global development blueprint.

provenance.sourcePolicy: Reference-frame vocabulary only. Psychology and development qualify orientation but do not redefine the Ascendant as total personality, appearance, mask, or independent actor.
